name: Fitness Story
_comment_group: The fourth show under the Snapchat heading, and the second one cut to
Hall of Femme's design. Everything that makes it a Snapchat pack —
the frame fetch, the vertical output, the transcription, the rewrite,
the card the caption is set on — is Hall of Femme's and is stated in
the same numbers. What makes it a different show is the two things
that are visible from across a room: the face the words are set in,
and the colours they are set in.
Written as its own folder rather than as an override of its sibling,
for the reason content/README.md gives: a channel is a folder that
gets dropped in. The prose below therefore points at hall-of-femme
wherever the reasoning is the same, and states its own only where

_comment_title: The whole of the difference between this show and Hall of Femme.
That pack sets its captions in Telegraf — a 200-weight hairline for
the block and the 800 for a picked word — on a hot pink card. This
one sets them in HK Grotesk, which the files themselves call Hanken
Grotesk, on an electric blue card: an ExtraLight Italic block, with a
picked word climbing to the ExtraBold Italic — the same two ends of a
weight axis, spent the same way round, in another typeface and on
another colour.
Four consequences follow from the face, and all four are worth
stating because they are what a reader coming from one of the
sibling packs will be looking for.
The first is that the card is doing the same job here that it does
next door, and has to. Hall of Femme's card and its hairline are one
decision: a 200-weight face over an unknown photograph disappears,
and the card is what makes that weight a choice rather than a risk.
A 250 is the same bet and gets the same answer. It would be kept
regardless, because it is the form this design IS — a statement laid
on the picture rather than words burned into it — and because the
colour pairing below is the show's look and there is nowhere else to
put it.
The second is that the whole block leans, and that is the show
rather than an emphasis. It is what separates this pack from the two
Open Sans shows next door, which set an upright block and pick a
word out by slanting it — here the slant is spent before the
highlight is reached, so the highlight has to be something else.
The third follows straight from the second: what is left is weight,
and this pack spends all of it — 250 against 800, the widest gap the
family has, which is Hall of Femme's 200-against-800 in a different
typeface. It is also the ONLY thing that changes across the card:
same slant, same colour, same size, flat ground, nothing else
moving. A cut that changed colour as well would be two signals
saying one thing.
The fourth is which END of that axis the block sits on, and this
pack has had it both ways round, so the reason is written down rather
than left to look arbitrary. It opened in the ExtraBold with a picked
word dropping to the ExtraLight, on the argument that the contrast is
exactly as loud either way because it is the same two ends. It is.
The two directions are still not symmetrical, and that is what
settled it: a 250-weight capital is the one setting in this family
with no stems to spare, and the frame opens on black type over
#0040FF, the darkest of the four cards. Run the other way, the
thinnest thing on the card was the picked word — the least legible
thing on the frame, which is an odd place for the word that was worth
picking out, and backwards from every other pack under this heading
(Hall of Femme 200 to 800, Fight Source and Determined 400 to 600).
The hairline is the block now, where the card is already there to
hold it up, and the emphasis climbs into the cut with stems to
spare.
An italic block is a real cost anywhere the type sits on a
photograph, and it is not one here. These letters are on a solid
card in a colour somebody chose, at 40px capitals, so the slant
costs nothing it would cost over an unknown picture — the same
argument the card already makes for the hairline the block is set
in.

_comment_color: The channel's own answer, and therefore what every frame is set
in until somebody presses a swatch: a frame stores no colour of
its own until it is given one, and this is what it falls back to
(see state.textColorFor). It is one of the four in `colors`
below, so the black swatch is the one that shows as chosen on an
untouched frame — the swatch is found by matching this value
rather than by being listed first.
Black letters on the blue card is the pairing this show opens
on. The blue is the brand, so it is the CARD — the shape that is
a fifth of the frame and reads before anything on it — and the
type is what has to stay legible against it.
Worth being honest about, because it is the one number here that
is not comfortably the best of its four options: #0040FF is a
dark blue, so black on it is a contrast of tone rather than of
brightness, and it is a smaller gap than black on the pink its
sibling opens on. It is the BLOCK this costs, since the block is
the 250: a hairline capital cut out of the card by a difference
of tone alone. That is the same bet Hall of Femme makes with its
own 200, and the reason both packs keep the card at all — the
argument is in `_comment_title` rather than twice here. The
picked words are the 800 and have stems to spare.
White on the same card is the louder pairing and is one swatch
away, and the other fourteen are beside it — which is the point
of handing the colours over at all.
_comment_colors: The four colours this show is set in, offered for the letters and
for the slab behind them — four buttons each in the title panel
(see editor.renderColorButtons).
The same four in both lists, deliberately, and for the reason
hall-of-femme states at length: the point is the PAIRING.
Sixteen combinations of an electric blue, an acid yellow, a white
and a black, and the ones worth having are the ones that read —
yellow on blue, blue on white, white on blue, black on yellow. A
palette of four colours that could only ever be used one way
round would be a palette of four cards, and this show's look is
the pairing rather than any one of them.
The blue and the yellow are picked to be each other's opposite
rather than each other's neighbour, which is what makes both of
them work in both roles. #0040FF is dark enough to be a ground
for the yellow and saturated enough to be ink on the white;
#FFF736 is bright enough to be ink on the blue and to be a card
the black sits on. Two colours of similar brightness would have
given eight pairings that are all the same pairing.
Absolute black rather than a soft near-black, and it is the one
colour here whose exact value matters. The other three are ink on
a card either way round; black is what the blue and the yellow
are loudest against, and a #111 that reads as black on a monitor
turns into a grey slab beside a genuinely black picture on a
phone. There is nothing for it to be too harsh against — the card
is a flat shape, not a photograph seen through it.
Nothing stops the user setting white on white, or black on
black. That is not an oversight: the two lists are independent
because the pairing is the feature, and a rule barring the four
matching combinations would cost the panel more explaining than
an invisible caption costs the user, who can see it is invisible
and presses another swatch.
`text` reaches the highlight as well as the block — see the note
on `colors` in js/channels.js. This channel's highlight is a
different CUT of the face and not a different colour, so what
colour the type is has one answer and not two.
_comment_highlight: Word scope, colour mode and what a second face costs are the
preset's — see snapchat-caption.json, which explains all three.
What this pack states is the two things that are its own: the
face a picked word changes to, and the colour it keeps.
The face is the ExtraBold Italic: the same slant as everything
around it, 800 against the block's 250. Why the emphasis is the
HEAVY end and the block the light one, and what the pack ran into
the other way round, is argued in `_comment_title` above rather
than twice.
The colour is the block's, so the recolour draws a picked word in
exactly what its neighbours are drawn in and the weight is the
whole of the difference. Stated all the same, for the fallback
reason `color` above is stated — and moved to black with it,
since a highlight that changed colour as well as weight would be
two highlights.
The two cuts are close in width, which is worth knowing rather
than assuming: measured at 40px, the ExtraBold runs 1.7% to 6%
WIDER than the ExtraLight across a caption's worth of strings —
fifteen pixels on a line of twenty-six characters, and six on a
single word. So picking a word out lengthens its line slightly
and the box behind it (cut to its own line's width, see `panel`)
steps out by about that much. It is small enough not to read as
the graphic changing shape, and it is the one direction worth
watching: a picked word near the end of a full line can push it
over the width, and at a stated size that is a rewrap rather than
a resize — the line breaks where the extra six pixels put it.
None of that is free under a size FIT, which would resize the
whole block to whatever the widest line needs and so retype the
caption around the word being emphasised. It is one of the two
reasons the preset's layout states its size instead.
_comment_panel: The card the caption is set on, in whichever of the four colours
the frame is wearing. Every number in it is hall-of-femme's, and
the long argument for each is there rather than repeated here:
one box per LINE and `joined`, so the background is a single
shape that steps in and out with the sentence instead of a
rectangle the width of its longest line; 12 of padding, which is
a highlighter's margin and not a card's; no border, because a
keyline would make the slab read as a box drawn over the picture
rather than as a card lying on it; 13 of corner radius, the
number every background under this heading is rounded by; and a
soft shadow falling straight down, which has to survive being
thrown by a white slab onto a white wall.
The fill is the one line here that is this show's own. The blue
is the brand and the card is the bigger surface — a fifth of the
frame, read before anything set on it — so the blue is the card
and not the letters. This and `color` above are also the only
place the opening look is stated: the two lists in `colors` are
written in one order so the two rows of buttons read as the same
palette twice, which means neither of them can decide what an
untouched frame wears.
